answers.answer: Dapper is a .NET micro-ORM/library that adds SQL execution and object mapping to application-owned ADO.NET connections, supporting synchronous/asynchronous access and buffered/unbuffered queries. Callers are client applications using connection extension methods such as Execute and Query; the README gives concrete examples. Repository consumers include Rainbow, EntityFramework handlers, SqlBuilder, tests and benchmarks (see q8). The README records Stack Overflow origins; it does not establish an exhaustive current deployment/customer list.

Dapper core supplies SQL execution/query mapping. CommandDefinition carries command text, parameters, transaction, timeout and flags, and creates/configures provider commands; DynamicParameters manages parameter bags. SqlBuilder assembles clauses/templates and their parameters. Rainbow adds CRUD helpers; EntityFramework packages provide EF handlers. ProviderTools offers provider-independent ADO.NET utilities and is currently non-packable. StrongName builds signed variants. Dapper.Tests is the functional suite; Dapper.Tests.Performance is the BenchmarkDotNet comparison executable.

Primary implementation is C# (shared LangVersion 13), with SQL supplied as strings. SDK-style .csproj files use MSBuild/.NET; Dapper.slnx organizes libraries, docs, tests and benchmarks, while Build.csproj uses Microsoft.Build.Traversal. build.ps1 provides PowerShell build/test/pack commands; YAML configures GitHub Actions. NuGet package identity follows assembly identity, with centrally managed versions in Directory.Packages.props. Core targets net461, netstandard2.0, net8.0 and net10.0; individual companion projects define their own targets. Dapper, SqlBuilder, Rainbow, EF and signed variants are separate project/package boundaries; tests and benchmarks are non-packable, as is ProviderTools at this pin. Markdown supplies documentation. This is an evidenced inventory, not an exhaustive language census.

The public entry is Dapper.SqlMapper.Execute(this IDbConnection cnn, string sql, ...), in Dapper/SqlMapper.cs:554. Optional param defaults to null. It constructs CommandDefinition with Buffered flags and calls ExecuteImpl.

SqlMapper.ExecuteImpl selects the single-command route; SqlMapper.ExecuteCommand implements its synchronous non-query execution, invoking the provider's IDbCommand.ExecuteNonQuery and returning that integer.

Dapper.SqlBuilder directly depends on the Dapper core project: its own csproj has ProjectReference Include="..\Dapper\Dapper.csproj". Direction is SqlBuilder -> Dapper, not the reverse. Source confirms concrete use of core DynamicParameters: ResolveSql constructs it; ResolveClauses calls AddDynamicParams to aggregate clause parameters. DynamicParameters is defined under Dapper/.

Normal-success path: Execute -> CommandDefinition -> ExecuteImpl. Null parameters make GetMultiExec return null, skip cache/parameter-reader construction, and reach ExecuteCommand with null reader. SetupCommand creates/configures the provider command. ExecuteCommand opens only an initially closed connection, calls ExecuteNonQuery, invokes OnCompleted, and returns the provider integer through ExecuteImpl/Execute. OnCompleted does nothing for null parameters. Finally it closes an initially closed connection, clears parameters and disposes the command. Dynamic boundaries: concrete IDbConnection/IDbCommand methods, provider-specific initialization and database execution are runtime-dependent; actual SQL, provider, server result and exceptions are unknown. No database execution was performed.

Direct project-reference consumers evidenced: Dapper.SqlBuilder, Dapper.Rainbow and Dapper.EntityFramework. Dapper.Tests also references core through tests/Directory.Build.props; Dapper.Tests.Performance through benchmarks/Directory.Build.props. Build.csproj includes core via its Dapper*/*.csproj traversal glob (build aggregation, not application consumption). Separately, Dapper.StrongName compiles Dapper/**/*.cs directly, so core source changes affect that signed build without a ProjectReference edge. EF.StrongName references Dapper.StrongName, not Dapper.csproj. ProviderTools has no core ProjectReference in its inspected csproj. This describes inspected project/build edges, not all downstream NuGet consumers or a proven runtime blast radius.

The README's non-result command example calls connection.Execute with a SQL batch that creates #t, inserts @a and @b with row counts enabled, then drops the table; anonymous parameters contain a=1 and b=2, and the example asserts count=2. It enters the public string Execute overload, then the single-command path (one parameter object, not a parameter sequence). This documented example is parameterized, unlike q7's null case; its assertion is documentation, not a trial execution.

Z enters as Execute's sql argument and becomes CommandDefinition.commandText, stored as CommandText. Without an explicit commandType, InferCommandType uses a regex: whitespace/reserved syntax (or null) yields Text; otherwise a simple name yields StoredProcedure. SetupCommand assigns CommandText and the inferred/explicit CommandType onto the provider command before parameter binding. In the null-parameter route no parameter reader rewrites the text; the provider receives it for ExecuteNonQuery. With non-null parameters, SQL also contributes to cache identity and parameter processing. For DynamicParameters, that processing can expand lists and replace literal tokens. SQL parsing/execution by the database remains outside this repository trace.
